t.2.86.2: Seeing Bharata, that tiger among men, approach with joined palms, the sage Bharadvāja, who had completed his Agnihotra offering, addressed him.
t.2.86.1: Then, having spent that night there, Bharata with his retinue, who had been received with hospitality, went of his own desire to Bharadvāja.
t.2.86.4: Bharata, having folded his hands in reverence and bowed low, spoke to that sage of supreme splendor who had come forth from the hermitage.
t.2.86.3: I hope the night passed pleasantly for you here in our domain. Tell me, O sinless one, were all your people fully satisfied with the hospitality?
t.2.86.5: O blessed one, I have dwelt here happily together with my whole army and its mounts, and you have abundantly gratified me and my ministers with every object of desire.
t.2.86.6: Rid of weariness and distress, well supplied with food and well sheltered, all of us, even the servants included, have spent the night most happily.
t.2.86.7: O blessed one, best of sages, I now take leave of you, if you will permit it; as I set out to my brother's side, look upon me with a friendly eye.
t.2.86.8: O knower of dharma, tell me of the hermitage of that righteous, great-souled one; declare to me which road leads there and how long it is.
t.2.86.9: Thus questioned, the greatly splendid Bharadvāja, of great austerity, replied to Bharata, who was eager to see his brother.
t.2.86.10: O Bharata, two and a half yojanas from here, in an uninhabited forest, there stands the mountain Citrakūṭa, with lovely ravines and woods.
t.2.86.11: Reaching its northern flank flows the river Mandākinī, overhung with flowering trees and bordered by lovely blossoming woods.
t.2.86.12: Immediately beyond that river lies the mountain Citrakūṭa. Their leaf hut is there, dear one, and there the two of them surely dwell.
t.2.86.13: O lord of the army, O greatly fortunate one, lead your host, thronged with elephants, horses and chariots, by the southern path, keeping to the left and to the right as well; then you will see Rāghava.
t.2.86.14: Hearing the word “departure,” the wives of the king of kings, though worthy of carriages, left their carriages and gathered around the brahmin.
t.2.86.15: Trembling, emaciated and wretched, Kausalyā, together with Queen Sumitrā, there clasped the feet of the sage with both her hands.
t.2.86.16: Her desire left unfulfilled and censured by all the world, Kaikeyī, filled with shame, clasped his feet.
t.2.86.17: Having approached that blessed great sage and circumambulated him, the one dejected at heart then stood close beside Bharata.
t.2.86.18: Then Bharadvāja, firm in his vows, asked Bharata: "O Rāghava, I wish to know about each of your mothers in particular."
t.2.86.19: Thus addressed by Bharadvāja, the righteous Bharata, skilled in speech, joined his palms in reverence and spoke these words.
t.2.86.20: O blessed one, this woman whom you see here, wretched and emaciated by grief and fasting, like a goddess, is the queen, the chief consort of my father.
t.2.86.21: This is Kausalyā, who gave birth to Rāma, that tiger among men whose gait is like the stride of a lion, just as Aditi gave birth to Dhātṛ.
t.2.86.23: Of this queen are those two sons, the princes radiant as gods, both Lakṣmaṇa and Śatrughna, heroes of true valor.
t.2.86.22: She who stands here clinging to this lady's left arm, downcast in spirit, like a branch of the karṇikāra tree whose blossoms have withered in the depths of the forest...
t.2.86.24: On whose account the two tigers among men have gone from here to the ruin of their lives, and King Daśaratha, bereft of his sons, has gone to heaven.
t.2.86.25: Know this Kaikeyī to be my mother, cruel and set on evil, ignoble though noble in appearance, and lusting after sovereignty, for in her I see the root of the great calamity that has befallen me.
t.2.86.26: Having spoken thus in a voice choked with tears, that tiger among men, his eyes red as copper, sighed again and again like an enraged serpent.
t.2.86.30: Then, having yoked the many splendid horse-drawn chariots adorned with gold, people of many kinds, eager to set forth, mounted them.
t.2.86.28: Kaikeyī should not be regarded by you with blame, O Bharata, for this banishment of Rāma will turn out to have a happy outcome.
t.2.86.29: Having saluted him and walked around him in reverence, Bharata, now fully prepared, took his leave and gave the command: “Let the army be harnessed.”
t.2.86.27: Then the great sage Bharadvāja, of great wisdom, replied to Bharata as he was speaking, uttering these meaningful words.
t.2.86.36: That army of Bharata, with its elephants, horses and warriors full of joy, terrifying the herds of beasts and flocks of birds as it plunged into that great forest, shone resplendent there.
t.2.86.35: That great army set forth, crowded with elephants, horses and chariots, covering the southern quarter like a great cloud that has risen, and passing beyond forests frequented by beasts and birds.
t.2.86.31: Young she-elephants and bull elephants, with golden girths and bearing banners, set forth trumpeting loudly, like thundering clouds at the end of the hot season.
t.2.86.32: Vehicles of many kinds, both large and small and very costly, moved forward, while the foot soldiers went on foot alone.
t.2.86.33: Then the women, led by Kausalyā, longing to see Rāma, set out joyfully in the finest of carriages.
t.2.86.34: And the glorious Bharata, mounting a splendid, well-equipped palanquin that shone like the newly risen sun, set out together with his retinue.
